slides.title: Meaningful play and agency
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm).
slides.picture: Step one: a thrown bola shatters ice. Step two: a chain from one action to the end of the game. Step three: eight routes through three forks, two players taking different ones.

new_texts: The player acts and the game responds in a way that matters.
The player acts and sees the game respond: the bola hits, the ice shatters.
why does this action matter overall?
Throw the bola: the ice shatters and the way opens.
Descriptive: the player acts and the game answers at once. The ice shatters, so the player knows the throw worked.

new_texts: The player steps back and asks why this action matters to the whole game.
FROM ONE ACTION TO THE END OF THE GAME
Evaluative: this one throw is 4 steps from finishing the game.
The player asks what the action means for the whole.
Evaluative: step back. Why throw the bola at all? Because it leads, step by step, to the end of the game.

slides.title: Risk versus reward
slides.source: Source: Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Net = 0.25 x 100 x score factor minus forgone points minus 0.1 x life value. All inputs illustrative.
slides.picture: Bars for points from invaders and from the UFO. Then three situations scored: reward minus the cost of going for it.

new_texts: A harder or riskier action pays more, and the player weighs the factors.
Average UFO score: 100 points, against 20 for an invader.
Invaders are worth 10, 20 or 30. The UFO gives 50, 100 or 150, and 300 on the 23rd shot. It is harder to hit, so the player takes a risk for a bigger reward.
all_texts: A harder or riskier action pays more, and the player weighs the factors.
Average UFO score: 100 points, against 20 for an invader.
Invaders are worth 10, 20 or 30. The UFO gives 50, 100 or 150, and 300 on the 23rd shot. It is harder to hit, so the player takes a risk for a bigger reward.

new_texts: A choice that changes what happens and that the player has to think about.
Behind on score, 3 lives, invaders far
Illustrative: 25% to hit, 100 average, 0.1 chance to lose a life.
The player weighs their score, their lives, and how close the invaders are. Same UFO, three different answers.

slides.title: Trade-off and persistence
slides.source: Source: Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Score curves are illustrative: 10 per second, a capture at 8 s, 20 per second after the rescue at 13 s.
slides.picture: A score line for a Galaga player who lets a ship be captured and rescues it, against one who does not. Then four power pellets spent across a stage.

new_texts: Give up one thing to get another.
the choice stays with you for a while
Safe: 10 points a second. Trade: lose a ship at 8 s, rescue it, then 20 a second.
Trade-off: in Galaga, letting the enemy take a ship costs a life, but rescuing it gives dual fire. The safe player scores slower after about 17 s.
all_texts: Give up one thing to get another.
the choice stays with you for a while
Safe: 10 points a second. Trade: lose a ship at 8 s, rescue it, then 20 a second.
Trade-off: in Galaga, letting the enemy take a ship costs a life, but rescuing it gives dual fire. The safe player scores slower after about 17 s.

new_texts: The player lives with the consequences of a choice for a set time.
Pellets left at the big group: 0
Spent early on the first four moments. No more until the next stage.
Persistence: there are only four power pellets. Use them on the first four moments and you face the big group with none.

slides.title: Situational choice and unit differentiation
slides.source: Source: Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Threat = hit chance x damage per second; the numbers are illustrative.
slides.picture: A grid of enemy behaviour and attack type, then bars ranking the threat from each enemy.

new_texts: Each enemy type does something different, which forces the player to prioritise.
depends on the player's own style
Each enemy sits in a different cell: 3 enemies, 3 different cells.
Imp: charges, fireballs you can dodge. Cacodemon: stays back, dodgeable. Shotgun guy: never misses. Each differs from the others on both counts.
all_texts: Each enemy type does something different, which forces the player to prioritise.
depends on the player's own style
Each enemy sits in a different cell: 3 enemies, 3 different cells.
Imp: charges, fireballs you can dodge. Cacodemon: stays back, dodgeable. Shotgun guy: never misses. Each differs from the others on both counts.

new_texts: The same choice is better or worse depending on the situation the player is in.
THREAT THAT YOU CANNOT DODGE (DAMAGE PER SECOND)
Illustrative: hit chance × damage per second.
With a shotgun guy and an imp in the room, the shotgun guy is the bigger threat, since the imp can be dodged. Remove him and the answer may change.

slides.title: Frustration, difficulty and fairness
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games??” Episode 10: Game Design; Crash Course Games, “Game Design”.
slides.notes: Expected attempts computed from the per-attempt win chances.
slides.picture: Chance of beating a boss on each attempt: it climbs when the player can learn and stays flat when the game is inconsistent. Then a grid of difficulty against fairness.

new_texts: Some is part of challenge; it has to be the kind the player can learn from.
whether you can learn from losing
CHANCE OF WINNING ON EACH ATTEMPT
Inconsistent (black): about 10 attempts, and nothing to learn.
Both players lose a lot. The first can see what to change and improves. The second cannot, so the chance never moves. Same frustration, very different games.
all_texts: Some is part of challenge; it has to be the kind the player can learn from.
whether you can learn from losing
CHANCE OF WINNING ON EACH ATTEMPT
Inconsistent (black): about 10 attempts, and nothing to learn.
Both players lose a lot. The first can see what to change and improves. The second cannot, so the chance never moves. Same frustration, very different games.

new_texts: Clear expectations and consistent design, so the player can learn from failing.
How hard the opposition is; it is separate from fairness.
Difficulty is how hard. Fairness is whether the player can learn.
A very hard game can still feel fair. When rules change or obstacles ambush the player, it feels unfair, and winning stops feeling earned.

slides.title: Luck and skill
slides.source: Source: “So You Wanna Make Games??” Episode 10: Game Design; Crash Course Games, “Game Design”.
slides.notes: 4000 matches each; outcome = luck weight x random + (1 - luck weight) x skill; skills 0.7 and 0.5; luck weights 1.0, 0.6 and 0.3 are illustrative.
slides.picture: Bars for how often a skilled player beats a weaker one in three games, from a seeded simulation of 4000 matches each.

new_texts: Luck: chance decides. Skill: the player's ability decides. Games mix the two.
HOW OFTEN THE SKILLED PLAYER WINS
Pure luck: the stronger player wins half the time, about 50%. It works for a game that needs no skill.
all_texts: Luck: chance decides. Skill: the player's ability decides. Games mix the two.
HOW OFTEN THE SKILLED PLAYER WINS
Pure luck: the stronger player wins half the time, about 50%. It works for a game that needs no skill.

new_texts: Battle royale: random loot, skilled fights
Mostly skill: the stronger player wins 86% of matches.

new_texts: A mix: 62%. A weaker player can still win with good loot, and a strong one can recover from a bad start. The weights are my own illustration.

slides.title: Balance and rock-paper-scissors
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm).
slides.notes: Win rate against a random opponent: 1 for a win, 0.5 for a tie, 0 for a loss.
slides.picture: A triangle of water, fire and grass with arrows for who beats whom, then bars of the average win rate of each option.

new_texts: Every advantage has a disadvantage; no role starts with an unfair edge.
Each option beats one and loses to another, so no option wins everywhere.
WATER BEATS FIRE, FIRE BEATS GRASS, GRASS BEATS WATER
average win rate against a random opponent
Each option beats one, loses to one. Against a random opponent each wins 0.50 of the time: balanced.
all_texts: Every advantage has a disadvantage; no role starts with an unfair edge.

new_texts: AFTER A CHANGE: FIRE AND WATER NOW TIE
Make fire tie with water and fire wins 0.67, water drops to 0.33. Nobody picks water any more.

slides.title: Downtime and probability
slides.notes: Exact dice probabilities; better of two rolls has P(total <= s) squared.
slides.picture: A timeline of four players taking turns of 15 seconds against 45 seconds, then two bar charts of dice results for one roll and for the better of two rolls.

new_texts: Time a player waits with nothing to do.
Short turns keep players in the game. With turns of 45 s instead of 15 s, each player waits 135 s instead of 45 s for their next go.
all_texts: Time a player waits with nothing to do.
Short turns keep players in the game. With turns of 45 s instead of 15 s, each player waits 135 s instead of 45 s for their next go.

new_texts: The odds of each result; extra rolls change them.
TWO SIX-SIDED DICE: CHANCE OF EACH TOTAL
Total 10 or more: 16.7% on one roll, 30.6% taking the better of two.
grey: one roll red: better of two rolls
Allow a re-roll and the odds shift: high totals become much more likely. This is why "no more than one roll per turn" protects the game's design.

slides.title: Before you call the choices done
slides.source: Source: Crash Course Games, “Game Design”; Game/Show, episode on interesting choices (title to confirm); “So You Wanna Make Games??” Episode 10: Game Design.
slides.picture: A checklist of six items drawn one at a time.

new_texts: Does the player see a response to each action, and why it matters?
Is there at least one real trade-off or lasting choice?
Do different enemies or options call for different answers?
Is the challenge hard and fair, so failing teaches something?
Is the luck and skill mix right for the game?
Is every option worth taking, and are turns short enough?
Then say it exactly: not “make fights interesting”, but “one enemy never misses”.
